clue.text: Newspaper cutting provides insight

indicators.note: the run of words provides, or yields up, the letters strung across the join between them

explanation.surface: A clipping from the paper gives you a fresh understanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'provides' signals a run of letters inside newsPAPER CUTting.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperçu is a brief illuminating glimpse or perception, a flash of insight.

clue.text: See 7
Country where Livingstone and Stanley finally meet? Away!

parts.note: Ken Livingstone, the former Mayor of London

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the explorer's surname

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for away in football results

explanation.surface: Where did the explorers Livingstone and Stanley meet in Africa?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes the explorers, but Livingstone is Ken Livingstone, a London politician; 'finally' takes the last letter of Stanley.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenya is an East African nation.

clue.text: Just taking one subject at school? Honestly!

indicators.note: the word for 'just' takes in, or holds, the school subject

parts.note: just means only
PE, physical education, is a school subject

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated that a pupil studies only one subject.
explanation.walkthrough: PE is the usual short form for physical education, a school lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something openly means doing it frankly and without concealment.

clue.text: Woman getting married shortly (around noon) is having one port

indicators.note: the shortened woman goes around the letter for noon
shortly says the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a bride is a woman getting married
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A bride about to wed at midday is having a drink at a port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' cuts BRIDE to BRID; 'around' puts N in it, giving BRIND.
explanation.definitionFit: Brindisi is a seaport on the heel of Italy.

clue.text: Time to cut old wood? Absolutely right

indicators.note: the letter for time is set to cut into the golf club's name

parts.note: a spoon is an old name for a lofted wooden golf club

explanation.surface: A forester decides it is time to fell some ancient trees, and is told that's exactly right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old wood' looks like timber but is the spoon, an obsolete golf club; 'to cut' puts T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot-on is British slang for exactly correct.

clue.text: Dutch doctor Robin lusted after

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the following letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A Dutch physician called Robin lusted after someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' is not Netherlands: 'old Dutch' is Cockney slang for a wife, and the answer is rhyming slang for wife too. 'doctor' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang for a man's spouse, which 'old Dutch' also means.

clue.text: Price I'm working for based on experience

indicators.note: the letters are put to work in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper names a price at which they will work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges PRICE and IM.
explanation.definitionFit: Empiric is an old adjective meaning relying on observation rather than theory.

clue.text: Carly uneasy about fancy men appearing during trial (she killed her husband)

indicators.note: the scrambled name goes about, or around, the rest
uneasy means unsettled, so the name's letters are disturbed
the jumbled men appear during, or inside, the trial

parts.note: a test is a trial

indicators.note: fancy here means elaborately rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman named Carly is nervous about her lovers turning up in court after her husband's death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' scrambles MEN to EMN; 'uneasy' scrambles CARLY into CLY...RA. The printed 'Early' is a misread: its E cannot appear in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth, Agamemnon's wife murdered him on his return from Troy.

clue.text: See 14
Lacking confidence, solvers abroad entering almost no answers initially

indicators.note: the foreign word for 'you' enters the trimmed word for 'almost'
no says the letter is removed from the word

parts.note: almost means nearly

indicators.note: initially picks the opening letter of the word

parts.note: solvers are 'you' to the setter, and in French you is vous

explanation.surface: A timid solver overseas, having nearly no answers at first.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the A leaves NERLY. The setter addresses the solver as 'you', which in French is vous.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting nervously means acting with anxiety and timidity.

clue.text: Vote against keeping news from nurse

indicators.note: the negative vote keeps the other letters held inside it

parts.note: nay is a vote against
read as new's, the plural of N, the abbreviation for new, so two of them

explanation.surface: A voter opposes withholding the latest reports from a nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'news' is taken as several 'new's, each abbreviated N.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanny is a children's nursemaid, someone employed to care for them.

clue.text: Drug book giving information on what's been added

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
Numbers is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A pharmacist's reference book listing additives.
explanation.walkthrough: E numbers are the codes printed on food labels in Europe and the UK for added ingredients.
explanation.definitionFit: The codes on a food label tell you which additives the product contains.

clue.text: Wed years, minds don't meet — fun involved with this clichéd 16? …

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so all these letters are mixed together

explanation.surface: A couple married for years who no longer see eye to eye, and the fun has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges all of 'Wed years minds don't meet fun'. The definition points to the next clue: the cliché is a straying husband's line about his marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A hackneyed complaint about a marriage, the stock line of a husband seeking sympathy elsewhere.

clue.text: Must I? She's in 7 … and 7/2

indicators.note: being in a state of difficulty, as the 7 down cross-reference says, means these letters are in disorder

explanation.surface: A reluctant husband asks whether he must take his wife along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in 7' is the anagram signal: the letters of MUST I SHE'S are in a mess. The definition is the full 7/2 answer, rhyming slang for wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are colloquial British terms for a man's spouse.

clue.text: … Went home only occasionally -"No fun at this flipping address!"

indicators.note: flipping means turning over and mixing up these letters
only occasionally means just every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: A husband who rarely comes home complains about his miserable household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only occasionally' takes the even letters of WENT HOME, ETOE; 'flipping' rearranges those with NO FUN AT THIS. The address is the US president's yearly speech to Congress.
explanation.definitionFit: The US president's annual speech to Congress is known as this kind of address.

clue.text: River in a European capital city

indicators.note: the river is set in the middle of the capital

parts.note: Bern is the capital of Switzerland
the Dee is a river in Scotland and Wales

explanation.surface: A river flowing through a continental capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the definition is 'River', but the Dee flows through the answer, a Scottish city, which is defined by the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberdeen is a city in north-east Scotland.

clue.text: Release son trapped by one hand

parts.note: 'un is dialect for one, as in 'a good 'un'

indicators.note: the letter for son is trapped by the word for a hand

parts.note: giving someone a hand means applauding them, a clap

explanation.surface: A boy held by one hand is let go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trapped by' puts S inside CLAP; 'un for one is informal, as in 'a big 'un'.
explanation.definitionFit: To unclasp is to undo a grip or fastening, setting something free.

clue.text: Listened to a sex programme

indicators.note: what was listened to was the spoken phrase, not the written one

parts.note: a gender is a sex

explanation.surface: Someone tunes in to a racy broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech, 'a gender' and the answer sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda is a schedule of items to be dealt with, a plan.

clue.text: See 14
Writing to return money — pounds

indicators.note: to return means the abbreviation is turned back

parts.note: MS, manuscript, is a piece of writing
ackers is old British slang for money

explanation.surface: Writing a letter to send back some cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' reverses MS to SM.
explanation.definitionFit: Smackers is British slang for pounds sterling, as in 'fifty smackers'.

clue.text: University about to finish last

parts.note: to finish means to end
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A student at university about to graduate, coming last.
explanation.definitionFit: To last is to continue or persist, to hold out.

clue.text: Complete dump by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word is judged by how it is spoken

parts.note: a dump is a hole, a squalid place

explanation.surface: A place that sounds like a total tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Something complete is entire, with nothing missing.

clue.text: Earl with daughter in 'Dog and Duck'

indicators.note: the daughter's letter is placed in the word for dog

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An aristocrat and his daughter drinking in a pub called the Dog and Duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog and Duck' looks like a pub name, but splits into wordplay and definition: 'in' puts D in DOG, and E (earl) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck something is to evade it.

clue.text: One economising rarely-burden has eased

indicators.note: eased suggests letters loosened and shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: A thrifty person sometimes lightens a burden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rarely' belongs to the definition: the answer is a rare word. 'eased' rearranges BURDEN HAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A husbander is someone who manages resources carefully, saving and conserving them.

clue.text: Constantly recurring outside — without sign something's wrong

indicators.note: without means the cross is taken away from the word

parts.note: external means outside
a cross, X, marks a mistake

explanation.surface: A persistent warning on the outside that something is amiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes X (the mark for an error) from EXTERNAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal can mean incessant or seemingly never-ending, as in eternal complaints.

clue.text: Bird, maybe one down under, keeping rent back

indicators.note: back says the whole assembled piece is read in reverse
the Australian bird keeps the tear inside it

parts.note: the emu is a bird from Australia, down under
a rent is a rip or tear

explanation.surface: An Australian bird retains a tear at its back.
explanation.walkthrough: Inserting gives ERIPMU before it is turned round. Dickie Bird was a famous English cricket umpire.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickie Bird was a celebrated cricket official, so he is an example of one.
